name: MARPE (mini-implant palate expander)

lead: MARPE widens a narrow upper jaw in late adolescents and adults without surgery. It looks like a conventional expander but is fixed to the roof of the mouth with small bone screws, so the force splits the palate rather than just tipping the teeth.

In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed for cheekbone width, midface support and breathing. A 2021 meta-analysis and CBCT studies report skeletal expansion along with some dental change in late adolescents and young adults. Published research covers bite and skeletal change; a trial of 3D facial soft tissue change and perceived appearance is registered.

paras: An orthodontist fits the appliance with two to four mini-implants and the expander screw is turned gradually over weeks, then held for months, usually followed by braces. Users on forums report costs in the thousands of dollars.

Reported issues include incomplete suture opening in some patients, tooth tipping, pain, soreness, screw loosening or failure, and expansion greater at the front of the palate than the back. It is a prescription orthodontic procedure; long-term stability and facial appearance studies are limited.

angle.text: Teens and young adults use MARPE to widen the upper jaw without cutting bone, and forum users hope for a broader midface and cheekbone support. Studies show skeletal widening for narrow jaws; cosmetic facial effects are barely studied.

lead: MARPE (micro-implant or miniscrew-assisted rapid palatal expansion) is an orthodontic technique for widening a narrow upper jaw in patients whose midpalatal suture is no longer easily opened by a conventional tooth-borne expander. Two to four mini-implants anchor the appliance to the bone of the palate, so the expansion force is applied to the skeleton and not only to the teeth. It is prescribed for maxillary transverse deficiency, a narrow upper jaw associated with crossbite, crowding and, in some patients, a constricted nasal airway [1][2][3].

For someone interested in their appearance, the appeal is a wider upper arch and midface: looksmaxxing communities discuss possible changes to midface width, cheekbone support, smile fullness and breathing [4][5]. Published studies measure skeletal width, tooth movement, airway volume and pain on CBCT scans and questionnaires; a trial of three-dimensional facial soft tissue change and perceived appearance after MARPE is registered but has not yet reported [6].

The technique was developed in the 2010s by Won Moon and colleagues at UCLA and has since produced case reports, imaging studies, randomized trials and several systematic reviews [1][7][8]. A named variant, the Maxillary Skeletal Expander (MSE), uses four bicortical mini-implants placed in the posterior palate [9]. Users on looksmax.org treat MARPE as a prominent non-surgical option in the 'hardmaxx' category, alongside discussion of surgically assisted expansion and jaw surgery [4][5][10].

paras: A conventional rapid palatal expander is attached to the upper molars and works well in children, in whom the midpalatal suture is still open. In older patients, researchers note that forces transmitted through the teeth can tip teeth and bend the alveolar bone instead of separating the suture, which prompted designs that attach to bone [2][11][12].

In MARPE, mini-implants are placed in the palatal vault and connected to the expander body, so that force is applied directly to bone. Designs differ in the number of mini-implants (two or four), whether they engage one or both cortical layers, and whether the appliance also clasps the teeth (a hybrid design) [9][13][12]. Finite element analyses have modelled how stress travels through the nasomaxillary complex with and without mini-implants [14][15].

Wikipedia describes MARPE as one of several approaches: tooth-borne rapid expansion, slow expansion, mini-implant-assisted expansion and surgically assisted expansion, with the choice depending largely on how mature the palate is [3].

Palatal expansion itself dates to the nineteenth century: Emerson Angell reported a screw expander in Dental Cosmos in 1860, and the Haas (1956) and Hyrax (1968) tooth-borne designs followed [3]. Mini-implant-supported expansion appeared decades later. A 2017 article by Brunetto, Sant'Anna, Machado and Moon credits Won Moon and colleagues at UCLA with developing MARPE as a less invasive alternative to surgically assisted expansion in non-growing patients [1].

The first widely cited publications were a 2014 finite element study of the stress distribution in the nasomaxillary complex [14], a 2016 case report of a 19-year-old with maxillary constriction treated without surgery [2] and a 2016 review of the quest for 'pure orthopedic movement' [11]. In 2017 imaging studies described changes in the midpalatal and pterygopalatine sutures with the MSE appliance and skeletal and dentoalveolar changes in young adults [9][16][17].

A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis searched seven databases for studies of MARPE in patients aged 16 and over and included eight articles, two prospective and six retrospective. Seven were judged at serious risk of bias and the certainty of evidence was graded very low. Pooled success was 92.5 percent, with a mean skeletal expansion of 2.33 mm and a dental intermolar expansion of 6.55 mm. Treatment produced increases in dental tipping and nasal soft tissue change and decreases in buccal bone thickness and buccal alveolar height, and expansion periods ranged from 20 to 126 days [7]. A 2022 umbrella review of four systematic reviews rated one as high quality, one low and two critically low, and concluded that MARPE appeared to give significant changes with fewer adverse outcomes than conventional expansion or surgically assisted expansion, while calling for better trials [8].

A randomized trial of 40 adolescents and young adults compared conventional expansion with MARPE using low-dose CBCT. The midpalatal suture separated in 18 of 20 conventional patients and 19 of 20 MARPE patients; MARPE gave greater nasal and maxillary width, less buccal displacement of anchor teeth and smaller losses during consolidation [18]. A trial of 60 post-pubertal patients (mean age about 15) found suture separation in 100 percent of MARPE and 86.7 percent of Hyrax patients, with first-molar expansion of 3.82 versus 2.20 mm and a skeletal-to-dental ratio of 61.4 versus 32.3 percent [19]. A 2022 systematic review of expansion in adolescents with permanent teeth (16 papers) concluded that MARPE was more predictable than Hyrax expansion and gave larger suture opening with fewer side effects [20]. A 2025 randomized trial of 30 late adolescents and young adults reported suture opening in 53 percent with conventional expansion and 60 percent with hybrid MARPE, with larger improvements in nasal airflow and skeletal width after MARPE [21].

A CBCT study of 14 young adults (mean age 20.1) measured expansion of 5.5 mm at the tooth crowns, 3.2 mm at the cementoenamel junction, 2.0 mm at the maxillary basal bone and 0.8 mm at the zygomatic arch, with buccal tipping of 1.1 to 2.9 degrees and decreases in buccal bone thickness of 0.6 to 1.1 mm [16]. A follow-up study of 24 patients (mean age 21.6) reported outcomes that were stable one year after expansion, with some relapse in individual measurements [17].

A retrospective study of 28 CBCT scans found success rates of 83.3 percent at ages 15 to 19, 81.8 percent at 20 to 29 and 20 percent at 30 to 37. Age was the only factor significantly related to success; all failures occurred in the more mature suture stages [22]. A comparison of 17 MARPE and 15 surgically assisted patients (mean ages 26 and 28.5) reported greater skeletal midface and posterior palate expansion and more parallel opening with MARPE, versus a V-shaped opening and greater buccal tipping with surgery [23].

Airway and sleep outcomes have been studied. A multicentre controlled trial in adults with obstructive sleep apnea reported an 85 percent success rate and a 65.3 percent improvement in the apnea-hypopnea index [24]. A controlled trial of 20 adults found total upper airway volume increased by 11.6 percent and 16.1 percent in two suture-maturity groups [25]. A randomized trial of 48 adults found that adding micro-osteoperforation reduced pain during expansion without changing airway gains [26].

Registered trials include studies of MARPE with and without corticopuncture [27][28], of two versus four mini-screws in non-growing patients [13][29], of speech effects [30], of sleep and airway [31], of skeletally anchored expansion in a 90-patient cohort [32] and of three-dimensional facial soft tissue changes and perceived appearance [6].

Authors of the reviews describe MARPE as effective for correcting transverse deficiency in selected late adolescents and young adults, and they caution that most included studies were retrospective, small and at risk of bias [7][8]. Reviewers pursue what one title calls 'pure orthopedic movement', a goal approached but not always reached because expansion is still larger at the teeth than at the basal bone [16][11].

Age and suture maturity are the factors most discussed. In one retrospective series success fell sharply after about 30, and the Journal of the World Federation of Orthodontists update reviews age limits and complications of non-surgical expansion in non-growing patients [22][33]. Expansion is larger at the front of the palate than the back because of the zygomatic buttresses, a feature noted for palatal expanders in general [3]. The 2021 and 2022 reviews also note effects on perioral and nasal soft tissue, which is one route by which expansion could alter facial appearance [7][8].
No published trial has measured whether MARPE changes facial attractiveness or cheekbone appearance; the registered soft-tissue and perception study [6] has not yet reported.

Reported effects include soreness and pressure while the screw is turned, tooth tipping, thinning of buccal bone, loss of alveolar crest height, nasal soft tissue change, incomplete suture opening and, in some trials, failure of the suture to open [7][18][22][21]. The Wikipedia article on palatal expanders lists speech changes and a lisp, extra saliva, pain and headaches, tongue sores and a gap between the upper front teeth as effects of expanders generally [3]. A registered trial is examining speech after MARPE [30].

Mini-implants can loosen or fail, and the procedure is a clinical one: the appliance is placed and monitored by an orthodontist. Posters on looksmax.org discuss downsides, including whether a wide face could look wider and whether results justify the expense [4][34].

On looksmax.org MARPE is discussed as a hardmaxx intervention, usually in connection with palate width, cheekbone projection, a fuller smile and breathing. Threads ask how to obtain it, whether it is worth a given expansion (for example 4 mm), how it compares with jaw surgery and how it combines with facemask treatment or braces [4][5][10][35][36][37][38][39][40].

One poster aged 15 reported that an orthodontist had predicted about 6 mm of skeletal expansion, from a 36 mm to a 41 mm palate, at a quoted cost of about 11,000 dollars, and asked whether that was enough; replies suggested asking for a larger target [5]. Another thread asks whether expansion would make an already wide mid face worse, with a reply warning that it could change the face's look [4][41]. These accounts are anecdotal and many come from teenagers and young adults describing their own cases or quotes from clinics.
Orthodontic literature frames the same procedure around crossbite, crowding and breathing, and published trials do not use facial attractiveness as an endpoint [7][18][19].

Related options include tooth-borne rapid palatal expansion in younger patients, slow expansion, surgically assisted expansion (SARPE) for mature palates, and orthognathic surgery such as segmental maxillary osteotomy [33][23][3]. Looksmaxxing discussions also place MARPE next to tongue-posture practices such as mewing, which proponents say gradually widens the palate; the studies above concern appliance-based expansion.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org MARPE is a frequent topic among users interested in midface width, a narrow palate and non-surgical alternatives to jaw surgery. Threads mix clinic quotes, personal updates and questions about age limits and expected millimetres [4][5][39].

timeline.event: Emerson Angell publishes the first paper on screw palatal expansion in Dental Cosmos [3].
Andrew Haas reintroduces his Haas expander in the United States [3].
The tooth-borne Hyrax expander is introduced [3].
A finite element study analyses stress distribution with micro-implant-assisted palatal expansion [14].
A case report describes MARPE correcting transverse maxillary deficiency in a 19-year-old [2]; a review discusses the quest for pure orthopedic movement [11].

CBCT studies report skeletal and dentoalveolar changes and suture changes with MARPE and the MSE; Brunetto, Sant'Anna, Machado and Moon publish a clinical article on non-surgical adult treatment [1][9][16][17].

A systematic review and meta-analysis of MARPE in late adolescents and adults is published [7]; a randomized trial compares MARPE with tooth-borne expansion after the pubertal growth spurt [19]; a CBCT study links success to age [22].

A randomized trial with low-dose CBCT compares conventional expansion with MARPE [18]; a multicentre trial examines MARPE in adult sleep apnea [24]; an umbrella review appraises the systematic reviews [8].

A Journal of the World Federation of Orthodontists update reviews conventional, surgical and miniscrew-assisted expansion in non-growing patients [33]; a controlled trial reports airway volume increases [25].
A randomized trial examines pain and airway changes with micro-osteoperforation [26]; a biomechanics review compares conventional and miniscrew-assisted expansion [12].
A randomized trial compares nasal airflow and skeletal change after conventional and miniscrew-assisted expansion [21].
